results.title: install a chained mirror fed by a trigger on the audit table
results.detail: schema, chained table, SECURITY DEFINER capture function, verifier and trigger created; 1 trigger now on auth.audit_log_entries. A tenant CAN attach a trigger to the Auth server's own table - the ACL grants postgres the TRIGGER privilege.

results.title: a real auth event reaches the mirror through the trigger
results.detail: admin user create -> HTTP 200, password login -> HTTP 200; the mirror captured the tagged entry 0s later. Mirror holds 4 rows (seq 1..4); verifier: 4 rows checked, first break none. GoTrue writes as supabase_auth_admin and the SECURITY DEFINER function still records it.

results.title: delete the LAST mirror row: does the verifier notice
results.detail: deleted the tail (seq 4) of a 4-row mirror; verifier reports first break none over 3 rows. Each row links to the one BEFORE it, so removing the newest rows leaves a chain that still recomputes end to end. A chain detects an edit or an interior removal; it does not detect truncation, and truncation is what someone hiding a recent event would do.

results.title: delete an INTERIOR mirror row: does the verifier notice
results.detail: deleted interior mirror seq 2 of 3 remaining; verifier now reports first break at seq 3 over 2 rows. A row removed from the middle cannot be removed quietly - the next row's prev_hash no longer recomputes.

results.title: the same identity rebuilds the chain and the verifier goes quiet
results.detail: rehash of every row -> true; verifier now reports first break none over 2 rows. The head hash moved from 5d462b0c1893... to 2eb685578caa..., so the ONE thing that survives an owner with a rehash loop is a head hash that was copied out of the database before the tampering. In-database immutability against the database owner does not exist; off-box anchoring is the control.

results.title: cleanup
results.detail: trigger and schema dropped (0 user triggers left on the audit table); 2 test user(s) deleted
